extracted.intended_audience: amateur and professional astronomers; readers of popular/educational planetary science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical principles for observing, mapping, and interpreting Martian surface features (maps, canals, polar caps) from telescopic data. Emphasizes methods of corroboration, geometry/projection conventions, seasonal/rotational inference, and physical diagnostics (e.g., polar cap composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescopic resolution principle
rubrics_metrics.description: With Mars discovery has from the start waited on apparent disk. To this end every optical advance has contributed from the time of Galileo’s opera-glass to the present day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optical improvements (increasing 'size of the eye') produce effectively a nearer view and allow progressively more particular and reliable mapping of the disk; observational conclusions must be tied to instrument capability and seeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential map comparison for corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps no vivider way of making this evident ... than by putting before the eye in orderly succession the maps made of Mars by the leading areographers of their day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare maps in chronological order to trace discovery progression and corroborate features; consistent inter-resemblance among independent maps strengthens confidence that markings are real rather than artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map projection and orientation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: They are all made upon Mercator’s projection and omit in consequence the circumpolar regions. In looking at the maps it is to be remembered that they are what we should call upside down, south standing at the top and north at the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Mercator projection customarily for Mars maps (take the equator as medial line); remember telescopic inversion (maps may appear 'upside down') and that circumpolar regions can be omitted or underrepresented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret observer variance
rubrics_metrics.description: None know better how surprisingly, even when two men have the same thing under their very noses to copy, their two versions will differ. Judgment of position and of relative size is one cause of variation; focusing of the attention on different details another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for human factors (judgment of position/size, attention to different details) when reconciling discrepancies between observers' drawings or maps; apparent disagreements may reflect emphasis differences rather than falsity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery periodization (three stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amid the remarkable continuity of progression ... we may, nevertheless, distinguish three stages in the perception of the phenomena: I. recognition of larger markings only (1840-1877); II. detection of canals intersecting the bright regions (1877-1892); III. detection of canals traversing the 'seas' and of oases scattered over the surface (1892-1905).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periodization to contextualize observations: earlier observers saw large markings, later ones finer linear features; interpret purported new details in light of improving seeing and technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing regularity as evidence of genuineness
rubrics_metrics.description: On comparing maps V, VI and VII an eye duly directed is struck by a difference in the aspect of the lines ... the geometrical character of the 'canals' was forced upon Schiaparelli by the things themselves, instead of being ... foisted on them by him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent increase in straightness/regularity of features across successive good-seeing observations can indicate that the eye and brain learned to distinguish real, repeatable detail rather than that the observer invented geometry; consider consistency across oppositions and observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation period determination from recurring features
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention shows these areographic features to be on hand with punctual precision for their traverse of the disk once every twenty-four hours and thirty-seven minutes ... we know the time they take to the nicety of a couple of hundredths of a second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine planetary day length by tracking punctual, recurring surface markings across the disk; repeated, timed transits yield precise rotation measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axis tilt and season inference from markings and polar caps
rubrics_metrics.description: We also find from the course the markings pursue the axis about which they turn; and just as the period of the rotation tells us the length of the Martian day so the tilt of the axis, taken in connection with the form of the orbit, determines the character of the Martian seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer axial tilt from the latitudinal behavior of features/polar caps; use measured tilt (≈24° here) together with orbital eccentricity to compute season lengths and asymmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar caps seasonal behavior as fundamental diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: The polar caps ... were early surmised to be of like constitution to Earth's ice and snow. Their varying size was subject to a regular rhythmic wax and wane timed to the course of the seasons of the planet’s year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat polar-cap size changes as primary indicators of planetary climate and seasonal state; their cyclical growth and retreat drive and illustrate other surface changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar cap composition diagnostic (water vs carbonic acid)
rubrics_metrics.description: At pressures of anything like one atmosphere or less carbonic acid passes at once from the solid to the gaseous state. Water, on the other hand, lingers in the intermediate stage of a liquid. Now, as the Martian cap melts it shows surrounded by a deep blue band which accompanies it in its retreat ... This badge of blue ribbon about the melting cap, therefore, conclusively shows that carbonic acid is not what we see and leaves us with the only alternative we know of: water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phase-behavior physics to diagnose polar-cap composition: presence of a blue band accompanying melt (indicative of liquid intermediate stage) argues for water ice rather than CO2 frost at low pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewing geometry affects polar-cap size measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: That we should first have known their smallest rather than their greatest extent with accuracy ... It has thus come about that both the south and the north polar caps have been repeatedly well seen and measured at their minimum ... minima are easier to measure because when a hemisphere is inclined toward the sun that hemisphere’s polar cap must melt and dwindle, while at the same time it is the one best seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for tilt and foreshortening: minima (caps near disappearance) are often measured more accurately than maxima because of viewing geometry; maxima can be underestimated due to horizonward foreshortening and pole orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terrestrial analogs for habitability assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The terrible necessity of water to all forms of life ... brings to one a deeper realization of what is really vital and what but accessory at best ... Merriam ... showed ... that the existence of a species was determined not by the mean temperature of its habitat but by the maximum temperature during the time of procreation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing habitability by analogy to Earth, prioritize availability of water over atmospheric pressure and consider peak temperatures during reproductive seasons rather than mean annual temperature as determinant for species survival and distribution.
